documentation: Paths in the public mirror targets that the corvidae transform must never write, and the keys it must not author inside the files it does write. Change detection in the mirror works by transforming into a clone of the target and asking git whether anything differs: an empty `git status --porcelain` means skip the sync. That only holds when this enumeration is exhaustive, so a missing entry degrades the mirror into 'always open a pull request'. `paths` is enforced by the guard in `target-owned.ts`, over a plan's writes and, since COR-1221, over its deletions. `insideFiles` states the ownership default for the structured files the transform does write — manifests and tsconfigs — which a whole-file guard cannot express; it is applied by `manifests.ts` and `typescript-configuration.ts` rather than by the guard. `targets` names the public repositories an entry applies to; omit it when the entry applies to every target.

paths.reason: Root license is repository-facing and target-owned. Evidence: weft ships a root LICENSE, cinder ships none at all, while every published package in both targets declares `"license": "MIT"`. A file whose presence differs between the two targets is not a transform output. Per-package LICENSE is transform-owned and stays writable: weft's `files` arrays list it and the transform fans it out to satisfy them.

Root README describes the public repository, its badges and its install story. Per-package `README.md` is deliberately NOT matched by this entry: corvidae carries a README in every workspace and the targets ship them through their `files` arrays, so per-package READMEs are transform-owned.
Contribution policy is written for the public repository's own workflow, which corvidae does not have.
Vulnerability disclosure policy for the public repository. Present in weft; absent in cinder.

Anticipatory, not evidence-backed: absent from both targets today. Included under the 'policy documents the target adds' class, because a public repository can add one at any time and corvidae will never have a counterpart.
Anticipatory, not evidence-backed: absent from both targets today. Same class as CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md.
Anticipatory, not evidence-backed: absent from both targets today. Attribution notices accompany a root license, so this is target-owned for the same reason the root LICENSE is.
Public roadmap. Present at cinder's root and in `labs/chat-room`; corvidae keeps planning in Linear, not in the repository.
Release history is generated in the target by its own release tooling (changesets in cinder, hand-maintained in weft) against versions that only exist downstream.
Changesets configuration and pending changeset files drive the target's release pipeline. Cinder carries `.changeset/config.json` and `.changeset/README.md`; corvidae has no changesets at all.

Workflows, composite actions, CODEOWNERS, branch protection and the pull request template are target-owned and composed separately. Corvidae's AGENTS.md forbids adding CI/CD here, so there is no corvidae source for them.
Git hook scripts. Both targets install husky hooks; corvidae explicitly has no Git hooks.

Weft's root `prepare` runs `husky && bun packages/weft/scripts/husky/verify-hooks-installed.ts`, so this hook-verification helper lives inside a package directory the transform otherwise writes. It is hook infrastructure, not package source.

The lockfile is regenerated in the target, not copied. Corvidae's lock resolves `applications/*`, `components/*` and `internal/*` workspaces that do not exist downstream, so copying it would produce an uninstallable target.

Ignore rules cover target-local build artifacts and tooling output (`dist`, `.turbo`, `.vercel`, `coverage`) whose layout is decided downstream. Evidence: the two targets carry thirteen `.gitignore` files between them, including per-consumer-fixture ones under cinder's `packages/components/fixtures/`, while corvidae carries exactly one, at its root. Every downstream `.gitignore` is therefore target-authored. If corvidae ever adds a workspace-level `.gitignore` as source, narrow this entry to the root rather than deleting it.
Worktree bootstrap list naming target-local non-secret files. Present in cinder.

Agent instructions are per-repository operating rules. Corvidae's say 'do not add publishing, CI/CD, deployment infrastructure', which is exactly wrong for a repository whose job is to publish, so they must never overwrite a target's.
Same as AGENTS.md: per-repository agent instructions with no corvidae counterpart worth propagating.
Repository-scoped agent skills. Weft carries fourteen, cinder two, corvidae its own set; none are package source.
Repository-scoped Claude Code configuration, agents and skills.
Repository-scoped Codex agents and environment definitions.
Repository-scoped editor rules.
Repository-scoped editor settings.

Coverage floors are target CI state, raised by the target's own runs. This entry is load-bearing rather than defensive: corvidae carries its own `components/chat/coverage-ratchet.json`, `components/cinder/coverage-ratchet.json` and `components/editor/coverage-ratchet.json`, so without it the transform would overwrite cinder's floors with corvidae's numbers on every single sync and the porcelain check would never be empty.
Target working document with no corvidae counterpart. See `openQuestions` on the one-off document class.
Target-maintained migration log keyed to published versions.
Target working document with no corvidae counterpart.
Target-maintained migration notes keyed to published versions.

insideFiles.policy: The ownership default inside a manifest or a tsconfig the transform writes, for a file the target ALREADY carries. COR-1223 inverted it. The transform used to emit corvidae's whole manifest and preserve a short enumerated list of exceptions; a live dry run against a seeded copy of the weft repository failed twelve of that repository's twenty checks, because the enumeration was a list of instances of a class it never named. Naming the class: the transform owns the *published surface* — what corvidae's source becomes once it is built and packed — and the target owns *everything that describes a repository corvidae is not*. So for an existing file the target's own copy is the base, the keys below are overlaid onto it, and anything not listed stays exactly as the target had it. A file the target does NOT carry has nothing to preserve, so corvidae's is emitted whole. The two enumerations that used to live here as `fields` pointers — `/version`, `/scripts/prepare`, `/devDependencies/husky`, `/lint-staged` — are subsumed: none of them is overlaid, so all four survive by default along with every key nobody thought to enumerate.

manifestKeys.reason: The public name is the mirror's own ruling, recorded in `package-map.json`. A target carrying a different name for the same workspace is a target the map has to be corrected against, not a fact to preserve.
Presence follows the disposition: stripped from anything the map publishes, forced on everything else. A published package that kept a stray `private: true` could never be released.

Root only, and the transform's because `layout-map.json` is what decides where each workspace lands. Preserving the target's globs would leave a workspace the transform emits — `internal/typescript` in the cinder target — outside the graph its own siblings resolve through.

Root only, and the transform's because it is computed rather than copied: corvidae's catalog plus one entry per cross-target edge the plan resolved. Preserving the target's drops those additions while the package manifests that reference them still say `catalog:`, which is a root the staged install cannot resolve. Absent for a target with no workspace root to hold one, where this entry then removes it.

The subpath map IS the published surface, regenerated from corvidae's source by `package-surface.json` and gated against the registry baseline by `checkParity`. Preserving the target's would let a subpath corvidae's source no longer provides keep being advertised.
The publish allowlist is computed alongside `exports` and checked against it by `checkTargetCoverage`; the pair only means anything when both come from the same pass.
Executable entry points are part of what a consumer installs, and `checkTargetCoverage` rules on them against `files` exactly as it does on `exports`.
A bundler's licence to drop unreferenced modules from the built artifact. It is a claim about corvidae's source, which is the source the artifact is built from.

manifestDefaults.reason: Legacy entry point. `package-surface.json` records it, but its own documentation says that record is a port of what the target publishes today — so where the target still carries the key, the target holds the authoritative copy of the same fact.
Registry access and tag are a release decision belonging to whoever publishes, which is the target's release tooling.
The runtime floor a published package advertises is a support commitment the target makes to its consumers; corvidae's floor tracks whatever Bun the workspace happens to run.

Peer ranges are a packaging decision, and they are only half of one: `peerDependenciesMeta` marks which are optional and is target-owned by default. Authoring one and preserving the other would let the pair drift apart.

dependencies.policy: Classification is the target's, ranges follow the package that declares them, and nothing is silently dropped. Three cases, applied to the union of corvidae's `dependencies`, `devDependencies` and `optionalDependencies` and the target's. `peerDependencies` is deliberately not one of them: a peer range is not a statement about what this package imports but half of a packaging declaration whose other half, `peerDependenciesMeta`, is target-owned outright, so it is listed under `manifestDefaults` and the pair is preserved or supplied together. (1) A package that ships from this mirror is the transform's outright — name, block and specifier — because only the transform knows what it is called downstream and whether the edge stays a `workspace:*`. Its stale entries are removed first, so an edge corvidae dropped does not linger. (2) A third-party package the target declares anywhere keeps the target's block and the target's range. Weft putting `better-sqlite3` in `optionalDependencies` and `peerDependencies` is a packaging decision of weft's; corvidae having it in `dependencies` is an artifact of being an internal workspace where every dependency is a plain one, and emitting that moves seven storage drivers into every consumer's install. (3) A third-party package the target declares nowhere is added in corvidae's own block at corvidae's own range, and reported as `addedDependencies`: a package legitimately gains a dependency, and the alternative to adding it is emitting source that cannot resolve its own imports. The asymmetry with `scripts`, which are never unioned, is deliberate: a dependency is a fact about the source, while a script is a choice about the repository.

insideFiles.typeScriptTargetOwnedPolicy: The keys below are read back out of the target's own `tsconfig*.json`; everything else in the emitted file comes from the transform. That is one key in practice, `extends`, and it is not enumerated because it is not a choice the transform makes per target: `@corvidae/typescript` is what corvidae's source is written against — `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` alone is why hundreds of weft files differ from upstream's — so the compiler options always come from the shared configuration, vendored where the target cannot hold the package. Enumerating it would be a list nothing reads.

typeScriptTargetOwned.reason: Which trees a repository type-checks is that repository's decision about its own working directories. Weft's `include` is `src` plus five named `scripts/*.ts` files; corvidae's is `src`, `tests`, `scripts`, `examples`. Emitting corvidae's widened it over the target's `examples/`, which import the package by its public name and resolve through `exports` to a `dist/` that does not exist when `typecheck` runs, and over the target's own `scripts/`, which it had deliberately never checked.
The other half of `include`; the two only mean anything together.

exceptions.policy: A temporary exception holds an additional path as target-owned for the duration of a transition, then disappears. Every entry requires all four keys: `glob` (the path held), `reason` (what transition requires it), `issue` (the Linear identifier that removes it) and `expires` (an ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` date). The guard fails when `expires` is on or before the current date, so an exception cannot rot silently — a reviewer must either move the date forward, which is a fresh review, or delete the entry. An exception without an expiry date is not reviewable and an expiry date without an issue is not actionable, so both are mandatory. Entries here are additive: they never relax a `paths` entry.

openQuestions: Root tooling configuration — `turbo.json`, `bunfig.toml`, root `tsconfig*.json`, `.oxlintrc.json`, `.prettierrc.json`, `.prettierignore`, `.stylelintrc.json`, `.editorconfig`, `.env.example` — is unresolved. Cinder carries four root tsconfigs where corvidae has one plus `internal/typescript`, so whether the transform generates these or the target owns them depends on the layout mapping, which is a different issue. Resolve before the first real sync run; leaving them out of `paths` is not a ruling that they are transform-owned. COR-1223 settled only the per-workspace `tsconfig*.json` the transform already writes, and only partly: `insideFiles.typeScriptTargetOwned` gives the target its `include` and `exclude`, while everything else in the emitted file comes from the shared configuration. What that discards is the rest of the target's own `compilerOptions`, which weft inlines rather than extending — `paths`, `rootDir`, `typeRoots`, `incremental`, `tsBuildInfoFile`, `assumeChangesOnlyAffectDirectDependencies`, `diagnostics`. None of them is load-bearing today (`@/*` is imported by nothing in either checkout, and the rest are caching and reporting), but the ruling is 'the shared configuration wins', not 'the target had nothing worth keeping'; a target that adds a compiler option corvidae's configuration cannot express reopens this.

One-off target working documents (cinder's `AB-429-final-contract-review.md` is the current example) cannot be enumerated ahead of time. COR-1221 settled what that means: the transform now deletes, but only beneath the paths it owns, which are the source trees it emits. A path outside those — a working document, a build script, anything nobody enumerated — is never deleted, so this class never needed enumerating. The enumeration itself is no longer write-only either: `assertDeletablePaths` runs the same list over a plan's deletions, so a target-owned path inside a source tree is refused as a delete exactly as it is refused as a write.
